definition: To spread out or scatter in different directions over a wide area.
example: When the concert ended, the audience began to disperse into the quiet side streets.
nuance: Disperse means to spread things widely apart, while its look-alike disburse means to pay out money.
prompt: A dandelion has gone to seed in a breezy field.
options: A gust of wind made the seeds disperse across the field.
The seeds disperse into a single tight clump beside the stem.
The seeds disperse by staying fastened to the flower head all summer.
The gardener used a new tool to disperse which weeds were dandelions.
reasons: The breeze carries the seeds off in many directions, scattering them widely.
Gathering into one clump is the opposite of spreading apart.
Seeds that never leave the plant are not scattering anywhere.
Telling weeds apart is discerning, a look-alike; nothing is being spread out.

practice.prompt: A student drops blue food coloring into a glass of still water.
options: After the lab, the student had to disperse of the blue water in the sink.
Within minutes, the dye began to disperse until the water was evenly blue.
The dye will disperse into one dark bead that sinks and never spreads.
The student began to disperse her partner's lab notes as sloppy and careless.
reasons: Getting rid of something is "dispose of"; disperse is never followed by "of."
The color spreads through the whole glass instead of staying in one spot.
Staying packed in a single bead reverses the idea of scattering.
Criticizing someone's work is disparaging, a look-alike word with a different meaning.
